newsitem.title: USA: Processed tomatoes could cut cancer risk-research.
newsitem.headline: Processed tomatoes could cut cancer risk-research.

text.p: Eating tomatoes and tomato products like ketchup and tomato sauce and paste could reduce the risk of developing prostate, digestive tract and other cancers, according to research released on Tuesday.

The key to the tomato's cancer-fighting prowess might lie in its red color, caused by a carotenoid called lycopene, investigators from the Harvard School of Public Health, the Dana Farber Cancer Institute, Tufts University, the U.S. Department of Agriculture and various European institutions said at a symposium in New York.
The symposium was sponsored by the Tomato Research Council and the American Health Foundation, which was founded in 1969 as a research organization devoted to preventing major chronic disease.

"Previous studies have already shown that lycopene...functions as a powerful anti-oxidant," said John Weisburger, director emeritus of the American Health Foundation and chairman of the symposium. "Other research suggests that lycopene is twice as potent an anti-oxidant as beta-carotene, its better-known cousin."

The human body does not produce lycopene, so the effect of this carotenoid can only be obtained through diet. Processed tomatoes -- the most abundant source of lycopene -- were better at the job than a fresh, raw tomato.
The amount of lycopene the body absorbed was also more important in lowering chances of getting cancer than the amount of lycopene consumed, researchers said.
The body absorbed lycopene best when tomatoes were heated using a small amount of oil, according to research conducted by Helmut Sies of the Heinrich Heine University in Dusseldorf, Germany.
"Lycopene appears to be more efficiently absorbed from sauce, paste or tomato ketchup than it is from raw tomatoes," Steven Clinton of the Dana Farber Cancer Institute said.
"Not only does processing concentrate the amount of lycopene present, but it has also been suggested that the small amount of lipid found in processed food may increase lycopene absorption," he said.
